newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq, U.N. agree on deployment of food observers.
newsitem.headline: Iraq, U.N. agree on deployment of food observers.

text.p: Iraq and the United Nations have solved problems holding up the deployment of international observers under their oil-for-food deal, U.N. and diplomatic sources in Baghdad said on Monday.
"If things go as planned all the observers should be in place by mid-March during which time we expect the first food shipments to reach Iraq under the oil deal," a U.N. source told Reuters.
The sources said Iraq agreed to permit 151 food monitors to use their own communications gear and move freely inside the country.

Iraq, they said, also dropped objections to the use of its Habaniya airport, about 60 km (37 miles) west of Baghdad, for flights by all U.N. personnel who will be involved in the implementation of the scheme.

"There is agreement in the communications sphere. We are now working on details. Transportation should not be a problem as we can use Habaniya airport for flights by experts working under the Memorandum of Understanding," the U.N. source said.
One diplomat said the two sides also reached agreement on the movement of observers whose main duty would be to ensure that food and medical supplies arriving in Iraq are distributed equitably.
One U.N. source said about 30 international observers arrived in Baghdad recently and were joined by 30 more international employees from U.N. agencies based in Iraq.

Iraq resumed partial oil exports worth $2 billion in December as part of a U.N. offer to mitigate effects of sanctions on the people of Iraq. Haggling over duties of food observers delayed the arrival of food and medical supplies for the Iraqis.

Diplomats said shipments of tea and detergents from Jordan under the deal would arrive in Iraq soon and they expected the first 100,000 tonnes of French wheat to be at Iraq's southern port of Umm Qasr by end of March.
"We are two to three months behind distribution. Working out the details of the Memorandum of Understanding is taking a long time," another U.N. source said.
Iraq needs 1.3 million tonnes of wheat flour, 319,000 tonnes of rice and 256,00 tonnes of sugar to meet needs covering six months.

More than $1.3 billion from the partial oil sales will enter Iraq's economy in the form of food and medicine in six months, relieving the government of the burden of paying about $100 million each month to subsidise the current food rations.

Revenues from the partial sale of Iraqi crude are being deposited into an escrow account and disbursed under U.N. supervision. Some 30 per cent of the money goes to a fund handling reparations for the victims of Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
